aphex-twin>can.note: This is Simon Reynolds's 1993 Melody Maker interview, republished by the Quietus. The page does not use the wording in the current citation. Reynolds writes that James has only recently retraced avant-classical and left-field rock, listening to Cage, Stockhausen, Reich, Riley, Eno and Can among others. James then says of 'all that stuff' that it is excellent. James also says that when he began making music he had never really listened to music and only later got interested in other people's records. So the page shows recent listening to Can, not Can shaping his music, and the direction is not clearly influence. Proposed: remove, or keep at critic tier only if recent listening counts. The citation needs rewriting either way.

galaxie-500>velvet-underground.note: Spin's 1989 interview (republished 2019) says Sterling Morrison's rhythm guitar on The Velvet Underground '69 is Dean Wareham's favourite on record, with no comment from Wareham on influence. Spin's standfirst says the band 'follow footsteps', which is the writer's gloss. In an AV Club interview (6 Aug 2010, https://www.avclub.com/dean-wareham-1798221180) it is the interviewer who says the Velvets' influence has been prominent since the beginning, so that is the wrong speaker. Wareham there only says he had a lot of VU bootlegs. I found no first-person statement that VU shaped Galaxie 500. Proposed: keep as a weak 'reported' fandom link, or leave as critic, and do not cite the AV Club question as Wareham's words.

galaxie-500>the-modern-lovers.note: The same Spin 1989 page reports that the band covered a Jonathan Richman song on their first album, Today. It also says the band call Richman the most underrated guitar player ever, and that their sympathy for the Modern Lovers 'makes sense'. That is a cover plus admiration reported by the writer, with no statement that the Modern Lovers shaped their music. Proposed: keep as critic or weak reported at most; do not present it as first-person influence.

radiohead>this-heat.citation: NPR Music (2020), on This Heat's "Twilight Furniture": "No, you're not listening to Radiohead in 2003 or Liars in 2006, but it's understandable if the obvious influence of This Heat circa 1977 makes you do a double-take."
radiohead>this-heat.note: The sentence is hedged. It opens by saying the song is not Radiohead in 2003, then speaks of This Heat's 'obvious influence'. The same article then calls such bands This Heat's 'apostles'. This is a critic arguing influence, not an artist or band statement. Coordinator: citation rewritten to the page's sentence; found is the full sentence as read prints it.

stereolab>this-heat.note: NPR's 2020 article says you can hear This Heat's tension in post-punk and art-rock, 'from Women to Stereolab to Deerhunter'. The old AllMusic citation was not used.

sonic-youth>this-heat.note: Two searches (Thurston Moore on This Heat; This Heat with Thurston Moore and Charles Hayward) found no statement that This Heat shaped Sonic Youth. The pages show only collaboration: the Moore/Hayward 2017 album Improvisations, and Moore guesting in This Is Not This Heat. NPR (https://www.npr.org/2020/08/21/904291487/understanding-the-impossibly-far-reaching-influence-of-this-heat) names Moore only as a guest. Wikipedia's This Heat page says critics recognise influence on Sonic Youth. I did not follow its footnote.
